items.readable_text:
Content:
To find the multiplicity of a root of a quartic polynomial, we can divide the polynomial by the corresponding factor as many times as possible.

Content:
For example, suppose we want to find the multiplicity of the root [MATH: x=-2] of the polynomial

Content:
[MATH: p(x) = x^4+2x^3-3x^2-8x-4.]

Content:
Because [MATH: x=-2] is a root of [MATH: p(x),] we know that [MATH: (x+2)] is a factor of [MATH: p(x),] which means [MATH: (x+2)] divides [MATH: p(x)] with no remainder. So, to find the multiplicity of [MATH: x=-2,] we will divide [MATH: p(x)] by [MATH: (x+2)] as many times as possible. Proceeding with synthetic division, we get

Content:
[MATH: − 2|1|2|− 3|− 8|− 4; 0|− 2|0|6|4; 1|0|− 3|− 2|0]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{p(x)}{x+2} = x^3-3x-2,]

Content:
which means that

Content:
[MATH: p(x) = (x+2) (x^3-3x-2).]

Content:
Now, let's see if [MATH: x=-2] is also a root of the cubic factor [MATH: (x^3-3x-2).] If it is, then [MATH: (x+2)] is a factor of the cubic, and we'll keep on dividing by [MATH: (x+2).] If it isn't, then we're done.

Content:
Substituting [MATH: x=-2] into the cubic factor [MATH: (x^3-3x-2),] we get

Content:
[MATH: (-2)^3-3(-2)-2 = -8+6-2 = -4 \neq 0. \quad \color{red}\times]

Content:
So, we are done. The factor of [MATH: (x+2)] has an exponent of [MATH: 1] in the factored form of [MATH: p(x).] Therefore, the root [MATH: x=-2] has multiplicity [MATH: 1.]

sections.normalized_html: Which root(s) of the polynomial [MATH: p(x) = x^4 - 6x^2 - 27] have multiplicity [MATH: 1?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. This polynomial is a biquadratic since all of the powers are even. So, we can let [MATH: u=x^2,] and factor the polynomial in terms of [MATH: u\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: p(x)|= x^{4} − 6x^{2} − 27; = (x^{2})^{2} − 6(x^{2}) − 27; = u^{2} − 6u − 27; = (u − 9)(u + 3)]

Now, we substitute [MATH: x^2] back in for [MATH: u] and continue factoring:

[MATH: p(x)|= (x^{2} − 9)(x^{2} + 3); = (x + 3)(x − 3)(x^{2} + 3)]

Note that the factor [MATH: (x^2+3)] cannot be factored any further, and it does not have any real roots.

The real roots of [MATH: p(x)] come from the factors [MATH: (x+3)] and [MATH: (x-3).] We find their multiplicities as follows:

  • The factor [MATH: (x+3)] has an exponent of [MATH: 1] in the factored form of [MATH: p(x).] So the root [MATH: x=-3] has multiplicity [MATH: 1.]

  • The factor [MATH: (x-3)] has an exponent of [MATH: 1] in the factored form of [MATH: p(x).] So the root [MATH: x=3] has multiplicity [MATH: 1.]

In conclusion, the roots [MATH: x=3,-3] both have multiplicity [MATH: 1.]

sections.normalized_html: Which real root(s) of the polynomial [MATH: f(x) = x^4+2x^3+x^2+2x] have multiplicity [MATH: 1?]
sections.readable_text: Which real root(s) of the polynomial [MATH: f(x) = x^4+2x^3+x^2+2x] have multiplicity [MATH: 1?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we need to factor the polynomial. Notice that all of the terms have a common factor of [MATH: x.] So, we can immediately factor out a [MATH: x] from all the terms:

[MATH: f(x)|= x^{4} + 2x^{3} + x^{2} + 2x; = x(x^{3} + 2x^{2} + x + 2)]

Now, we factor the cubic by grouping, and simplify until the polynomial is fully factored:

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
To find the multiplicity of a root of a quartic polynomial, we can divide the polynomial by the corresponding factor as many times as possible.

Content:
For example, suppose we want to find the multiplicity of the root [MATH: x=-2] of the polynomial

Content:
[MATH: p(x) = x^4+2x^3-3x^2-8x-4.]

Content:
Because [MATH: x=-2] is a root of [MATH: p(x),] we know that [MATH: (x+2)] is a factor of [MATH: p(x),] which means [MATH: (x+2)] divides [MATH: p(x)] with no remainder. So, to find the multiplicity of [MATH: x=-2,] we will divide [MATH: p(x)] by [MATH: (x+2)] as many times as possible. Proceeding with synthetic division, we get

Content:
[MATH: − 2|1|2|− 3|− 8|− 4; 0|− 2|0|6|4; 1|0|− 3|− 2|0]

Content:
Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac{p(x)}{x+2} = x^3-3x-2,]

Content:
which means that

Content:
[MATH: p(x) = (x+2) (x^3-3x-2).]

Content:
Now, let's see if [MATH: x=-2] is also a root of the cubic factor [MATH: (x^3-3x-2).] If it is, then [MATH: (x+2)] is a factor of the cubic, and we'll keep on dividing by [MATH: (x+2).] If it isn't, then we're done.

Content:
Substituting [MATH: x=-2] into the cubic factor [MATH: (x^3-3x-2),] we get

Content:
[MATH: (-2)^3-3(-2)-2 = -8+6-2 = -4 \neq 0. \quad \color{red}\times]

Content:
So, we are done. The factor of [MATH: (x+2)] has an exponent of [MATH: 1] in the factored form of [MATH: p(x).] Therefore, the root [MATH: x=-2] has multiplicity [MATH: 1.]

Item 2 — Example: Determining the Multiplicity of a Root of a Quartic Polynomial Using the Factor Theorem

Example Prompt:
What is the multiplicity of the root [MATH: x=3] of [MATH: p(x) = x^4 - 3 x^3 - 7 x^2 + 15 x + 18?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Since [MATH: x=3] is a root of [MATH: p(x),] the factor theorem tells us that [MATH: (x-3)] is a factor of [MATH: p(x).]

Because [MATH: (x-3)] is a factor of [MATH: p(x),] we know that [MATH: (x-3)] divides [MATH: p(x).] So, to begin factoring [MATH: p(x),] we can divide it by [MATH: (x-3)] using synthetic division:

| | [MATH: x^4] | [MATH: x^3] | [MATH: x^2] | [MATH: x^1] | [MATH: x^0] |
| [MATH: \color{red}3] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: -3] | [MATH: -7] | [MATH: 15] | [MATH: 18] |
| | [MATH: \color{gray}\downarrow] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: -21] | [MATH: -18] |
| | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: -7] | [MATH: -6] | [MATH: 0] |

Therefore,

[MATH: \dfrac{p(x)}{x-3} = x^3 - 7x - 6]

which means that

[MATH: p(x) = (x-3) (x^3 - 7x - 6).]

Let's check if [MATH: x=3] is also a root of [MATH: (x^3-7x-6).] Substituting, we get

[MATH: 3^3 - 7(3) - 6 = 27 - 21 - 6 = 0. \quad \color{green}\checkmark]

So [MATH: x=3] is indeed a root of [MATH: (x^3-7x-6),] we have that [MATH: (x-3)] is a factor of [MATH: (x^3-7x-6),] and we can continue factoring using synthetic division:

| | [MATH: x^3] | [MATH: x^2] | [MATH: x^1] | [MATH: x^0] |
| [MATH: \color{red}3] | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 0] | [MATH: -7] | [MATH: -6] |
| | [MATH: \color{gray}\downarrow] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 9] | [MATH: 6] |
| | [MATH: 1] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: 2] | [MATH: 0] |

Therefore,

[MATH: \dfrac{x^3-7x-6}{x-3} = x^2 + 3x + 2 ,]

which means that

[MATH: x^3-7x-6 = (x-3)(x^2 + 3x + 2).]

So we have

[MATH: p(x)|= (x − 3)(x^{3} − 7x − 6); = (x − 3)(x − 3)(x^{2} + 3x + 2); = (x − 3)^{2}(x + 1)(x + 2).]

The factor [MATH: (x-3)] has an exponent of [MATH: 2] in the factored form of [MATH: p(x).] So the root [MATH: x=3] has multiplicity [MATH: 2.]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Factoring Using Other Techniques

Content:
To find the multiplicity of a root, we have been using synthetic division. However, there are sometimes other ways to factor polynomials besides synthetic division. For example, remember that when a polynomial is a biquadratic, we can factor it as though it were a quadratic.

Content:
For example, consider the polynomial [MATH: p(x) = x^4 - 3x^2 - 4.] To factor this polynomial, we can let [MATH: u=x^2,] and factor the polynomial in terms of [MATH: u\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: p(x)|= x^{4} − 3x^{2} − 4; = (x^{2})^{2} − 3(x^{2}) − 4; = u^{2} − 3u − 4; = (u − 4)(u + 1)]

Content:
Now, we substitute [MATH: x^2] back in for [MATH: u] and continue factoring:

Content:
[MATH: p(x)|= (x^{2} − 4)(x^{2} + 1); = (x + 2)(x − 2)(x^{2} + 1)]

- The factor [MATH: (x-3)] has an exponent of [MATH: 1] in the factored form of [MATH: p(x).] So the root [MATH: x=3] has multiplicity [MATH: 1.]
